title: Plant Reproduction
seo_title: Year 7 Science: Plant Reproduction Worksheets (Pollination, Fertilisation, Seed Dispersal)
standard_text: Reproduction in plants, including flower structure, wind and insect pollination, fertilisation, seed and fruit formation and dispersal, including quantitative investigation of some dispersal mechanisms.
meta_desc: Free Year 7 science worksheets on plant reproduction: flower structure, insect and wind pollination, fertilisation, seeds and fruits, and seed dispersal investigations. 100 questions with answers.
key_sub: Ovules become seeds; the ovary becomes the fruit.
body_html:
How to think about it

Flowers are the reproductive organs of flowering plants.

  • Stamen (male): anther and filament. Carpel (female): stigma, style and ovary.
  • Pollination moves pollen to a stigma (by insects or wind). Fertilisation joins the pollen nucleus with an ovule nucleus.
  • Ovules become seeds and the ovary becomes the fruit. Seeds are dispersed by wind, animals, water or explosion.
Example

Pollination or fertilisation: pollen lands on the stigma?

Transfer of pollen

Answer: pollination

Example

What does the ovary become?

It surrounds the seeds

Answer: the fruit

Common mistakes

  • Thinking pollination and fertilisation are the same.
  • Thinking the stigma makes pollen.
  • Thinking wind-pollinated flowers are brightly coloured.

faq.q: What is the difference between pollination and fertilisation?
faq.a: Pollination is the transfer of pollen to a stigma. Fertilisation happens later, when the pollen nucleus joins with an ovule nucleus inside the ovary.

faq.q: How are wind- and insect-pollinated flowers different?
faq.a: Insect-pollinated flowers have bright petals, scent and nectar. Wind-pollinated flowers are small and dull, with lots of light pollen and feathery stigmas.
By wind (sycamore, dandelion), animals (berries, burrs), water (coconut) or by pods bursting open (peas, gorse).

items.q: "Pollen lands on the sticky stigma (pollination)." What happens next?
